text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Root cause: the most probable failure is an intermittent open circuit within the PGM-FI main relay, preventing the fuel pump from priming and the ECM from powering up consistently. The classic Honda “crank-no-start in rain” scenario matches cracked solder joints on the main relay PCB inside the under-dash fuse/relay box. Moisture or humidity can cause the cracked joints to separate enough to interrupt the ground or power path, yet once the vehicle warms up the connection re-establishes itself and the engine runs fine. No error codes is typical because the event is transient — the ECM never sees a running fault that stays present long enough to set a DTC. The new battery and starter eliminate the obvious no-crank scenarios; the inconclusive alternator test is a red herring because the alternator has nothing to do with an intermittent no-start when the engine is not yet running.
- Component failure analysis: Honda integrated the main relay into the driver’s under-dash fuse/relay box (MICU) starting in 2006. The original solder joints on the relay coil pins and the larger power-switching contacts are prone to thermal and vibration fatigue, leading to microscopic cracks. When the cabin is damp (rainy weather), the cracks can oxidize and the gap widens enough to prevent the relay coil from pulling in. This stops the fuel pump from running during the initial key-on prime cycle, and the ECM will not energize the injectors or ignition until it sees a valid cam/crank sync. The condition clears itself once the interior heat or a bump reseats the cracked joint. Because this is not a sensor or actuator fault, the OBD-II system does not log any misfire, fuel trim, or circuit codes during the failed start attempt — the ECM and fuel pump simply never wake up.
- Age/mileage considerations: At 16 years old, a 2009 Civic is deep into the failure window for solder-joint degradation, regardless of mileage. This issue is rarely influenced by engine run time; it’s a pure age, thermal cycling, and humidity-driven failure. The fact that it “happens randomly in rain” aligns perfectly with community-reported patterns spanning 2006–2011 Civics.
- Data Needed: Confidence is 65% — below the 80% threshold because the diagnosis relies heavily on symptom pattern recognition without hard test data. To reach a conclusive determination, the following must be obtained:
  - Audio/video verification or technician witness of the fuel pump not priming: turn key to ON (not start); the pump should hum for 2 seconds. Record this and note if it fails to hum when the problem occurs.
  - A “tap test” result: when the no-start is present, firmly tap the left side of the dashboard near the hood-release panel (the area of the under-dash fuse box). If the pump suddenly primes and the car starts, the relay is confirmed.
  - A scan tool snapshot during a failed crank: monitor RPM signal (from the crank sensor) and Main Relay control command using a professional scan tool that can read Honda PIDs. Confirm RPM shows ~150–250 RPM while cranking and that the ECM is commanding the main relay ON — yet the pump is silent.
  - Direct voltage measurement at the fuel pump connector during a no-start event: should see battery voltage for the initial 2-second prime; absence means the main relay or its ground side is open.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Crank position (CKP) sensor intermittent open when wet (medium likelihood): Moisture can infiltrate the connector or sensor body, causing a dropout of the RPM signal. If the ECM does not see cranking RPM, it will not command spark or fuel. However, an intermittent CKP signal often sets a pending P0335 or P0339 before a hard code, and many 8th-gen Civics do not exhibit this; instead, a water-damaged CKP usually causes a persistent no-start after driving through deep puddles, not a random rain correlation while parked. The engine would also stall while driving if the sensor failed momentarily, but the customer states it “runs fine once started,” which lowers CKP likelihood.
- Ignition switch electrical contacts wear (low-medium likelihood): A worn ignition switch can cause intermittent loss of power to the main relay coil or ECM. Rain/humidity could theoretically affect the contact resistance. This fault typically shows up as random stalling while driving or complete electrical shutdown, not just a crank-no-start. The customer reports no warning lamps or other electrical glitches, and the starter cranks strongly every time, suggesting the ignition switch’s START and ON contacts are functional. This remains a distant possibility best ruled out by voltage-probing the IG1 feed to the main relay during a failure.
- ECM/PCM internal ground corrosion (low likelihood): The ECM is located behind the glove box; a leaky cabin filter housing or windshield seal can sometimes drip onto the connector. If moisture corrodes a ground pin, intermittent no-start could occur. However, this usually produces multiple unrelated codes, erratic gauge behavior, or communication errors. The absence of any DTCs makes this unlikely.
- Fuel pump failure hot-soak or intermittent (very low likelihood): A failing pump motor can refuse to spin when cold or after a heat soak, but rain correlation is implausible. The customer says the car runs fine once started, and there is no extended crank time or stalling under load. Replacing the pump without confirming missing voltage at the pump connector would be a parts-cannon mistake.
- Aftermarket alarm/remote start system parasitic drain (low likelihood): If the vehicle has an aftermarket security system, moisture intrusion into its control module or wiring could inhibit the fuel pump relay control. No modifications were reported, but it is worth a quick visual check under the dash for non-factory wiring and a parasitic draw test. If found, completely disconnect the system and retest.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- The shop must perform a series of precise, low-cost tests before committing to any parts replacement. The goal is to isolate whether the fuel pump command is reaching the pump, and if not, where the circuit is breaking.
  - Test 1: Key-on fuel pump prime verification. With a technician or the customer cycling the key while the other listens at the fuel filler neck or rear seat bottom, confirm the pump runs for the expected 2-second prime. If absent, proceed immediately to Test 2.
  - Test 2: Dashboard “tap test”. Using a rubber mallet or the side of a closed fist, sharply tap the lower dash panel on the driver’s side, directly over the under-dash fuse/relay box. Then re-check for the pump prime. If the pump suddenly energizes, the main relay is the confirmed culprit. This test costs zero dollars and seconds of time.
  - Test 3: Scan tool cranking data capture. Using a Honda-compatible scanner (HDS, Snap-on, Autel, etc.), connect to the DLC and select live data: observe Engine RPM, Main Relay (also labeled “Fuel Pump Relay” or “PGM-FI Main Relay”) status, and Battery Voltage. Crank the engine during a no-start event. Expected values: RPM 150–250, Main Relay command ON, battery voltage above 10.5 V. If RPM is present but the relay command is OFF or the fuel pump does not run despite the command, the ECM or relay circuit is faulty. Typical diagnostic time for this capture: 0.5 hr, $60–90.
  - Test 4: Fuel pump connector voltage back-probe. Access the four-pin connector at the fuel pump (under the rear seat cushion). Back-probe the power (typically a thick yellow/green wire) and ground with a multimeter. During key-on, voltage must appear for the prime cycle. If voltage is missing, work backward to the main relay output. If voltage is present but pump silent, the pump itself is faulty, but this is not the primary suspicion.
  - Test 5: Main relay power and ground integrity. Remove the under-dash fuse box cover, locate the main relay (often labeled “FI Main” on the cover sticker). With the relay de-energized, measure resistance between the relay ground pin and chassis ground; must be 0.1 ohm or less. Check that battery voltage is present at the relay coil power pin with the key on. Intermittent failures may require wiggling the harness or heating/cooling the relay with a hairdryer and cold spray to replicate the fault.
- Estimated testing costs: a competent shop should be able to execute Tests 1 through 3 within a 0.5-hour diagnostic session ($60–100). Tests 4 and 5 may add another 0.5-hour if needed. Total diagnostic verification should not exceed $200 before any repair authorization.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- The following five technical questions are designed to expose whether the shop has actually performed Honda-specific diagnostic steps or is simply throwing parts at the symptom. Ask each question calmly and note their response.
  - “When you tried to duplicate the no-start, did you listen for the fuel pump prime? Specifically, was there that 2-second hum when the key first hits ON?” A knowledgeable Honda tech will instantly recognize this as the first check; a vague answer like “the fuel system checks out” is a red flag.
  - “Did you tap the under-dash fuse box during a failed start attempt to see if the main relay closes? Can you show me the result?” This question separates those who know the classic Honda fix from those ordering an entire fuse box assembly without simple verification.
  - “What were the cranking RPM and Main Relay PID status on the scan tool during the crank-no-start event? Can I see a screenshot or the freeze-frame data?” They must produce actual numbers, not just say “no codes.” If they didn’t capture live data during a failure, no diagnostic has been performed.
  - “Why is the alternator being tested for an intermittent no-start that happens before the engine runs? Walk me through how the alternator output would prevent the engine from firing during cranking.” The alternator is irrelevant during cranking; any shop pushing an alternator replacement is misdiagnosing. Listen for scientific reasoning, not “we’re just checking the charging system.”
  - “What’s the labor and part number for the main relay replacement on this VIN? Are you planning to re-solder the relay or replace the whole fuse box, and why?” This reveals if they’ve researched the correct repair path. The correct answer involves either a known re-soldering technique (with flux and high-heat soldering) or a specific MICU part number. If they quote a fuel pump, ignition coils, or an alternator, they are guessing.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: Enter the shop with a notebook and a calm, curious tone. Say, “I appreciate you looking at my Civic. I’ve done some reading on these intermittent rain-related no-starts in Civics, and I’d like to understand what testing you’ve done so far. Can you walk me through how you verified the fuel pump prime during the failure?”
- Phrasing: Frame questions as if you’re trying to learn, not accuse. Use phrases like “Help me understand…” or “I’m curious about…”. For example: “I’m curious—when you had the no-start, did you try tapping the dash near the fuse box? I read that sometimes helps narrow things down on older Hondas. What did you find?”
- Example dialogue for the alternator point: “I notice the work order mentions an inconclusive alternator test. I’m trying to wrap my head around that—since the engine wasn’t running during the no-start, how would the alternator be involved? Could you explain the theory there?” Their answer should be honest: “It wasn’t — we just ruled it out.” If they insist on an alternator, it’s a red flag.
- Body language: Maintain eye contact, nod to show you’re listening, and avoid crossing your arms. Keep your voice even. You are a person who authorizes work based on data, not a confrontational expert.
- Response handling: If the service advisor gets defensive (“Look, we know what we’re doing”), you can say, “I’m sure you do, and I’m not questioning your ability. I just like to approve repairs step-by-step with clear test results. Could we start with that key-on fuel pump prime test now? I’ll wait.” This keeps the interaction productive.
- Exit strategy: If the shop refuses to perform the simple verification tests or insists on a major repair without data, say, “Thank you for your time. I’d like to review the options. Please email me the line-by-line quote and the diagnostic notes you have so far, and I’ll let you know how I’d like to proceed.” This gets you out and gives you a written record.
- NEVER say: “My AI report says” or “I got a second opinion online.” Instead: “I’ve done some research on Honda forums and service bulletins, and I want to understand the path you’re taking.”

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Fair parts pricing: The PGM-FI main relay is integrated into the under-dash fuse/relay box (MICU). The OEM Honda part number for the entire assembly varies by trim but is typically 38200-SNA-A11 or similar, retailing between $280 and $380 at a dealer parts counter. However, the relay itself is a discrete component on the PCB, and many specialized electronics repair shops or skilled DIYers can re-solder the cracked joints for $30–80 in labor, with zero parts cost (just solder). A new, non-OEM aftermarket fuse box is NOT recommended due to quality and compatibility risks; the re-solder route is widely accepted as a permanent fix if done properly. If the vehicle must have a dealer-fresh assembly, budget $300–400 for the part.
- Labor hours: For a re-solder repair, a competent technician will remove the lower dash panel and the fuse box (0.5–0.7 hr), disassemble it, re-solder the relay pins (0.3–0.5 hr), and reinstall (0.5 hr). Total book time approximately 1.3–1.8 hours. At a typical independent shop labor rate of $100–$140 per hour, labor should be $130–$252. For a full MICU replacement, labor is slightly less, around 1.0–1.5 hours, because no soldering is involved; just R&R.
- Total price range: For the re-solder repair at an independent Honda specialist: $160–$332. For a dealer replacement of the MICU: $380–$550 parts + 1.0–1.5 hr labor ($130–$210) = $510–$760. Any quote exceeding $800 for this known issue, especially bundled with a fuel pump or alternator, is a massive overcharge.
- Overcharge identification markers: A shop quoting a new fuel pump assembly ($350–$600 part), a new alternator ($250–$450), or an ECM reflash/replacement ($800+) for a crank-no-start that is not accompanied by a hard DTC or a confirmed fuel pressure drop is not following evidence-based diagnostics. If they want to replace the entire under-dash fuse box without attempting or even discussing the re-solder path, they may be ignoring a cost-saving standard repair.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts cannon indicators: A quote that includes a fuel pump, fuel filter (non-serviceable on this model), crankshaft sensor, and an alternator — especially without a confirmed test result — is a classic parts cannon. The “new battery and starter” already done could be an earlier misdiagnosis; now the shop may double down. If they suggest a full fuel injection cleaning or a “tune-up” as the solution, it’s a money grab.
- Diagnostic shortcuts to watch for: If the shop’s entire diagnosis consisted of “scanned it, no codes, so it must be the fuel pump,” they skipped the most basic active tests. A 10-minute code scan does not equal a diagnosis. Demand to see the live data or the results of the prime test. Any shop that won’t show you the test results is likely selling parts, not repairs.
- Price gouging red flags: An OEM MICU priced above $600, or a re-solder job quoted at 3+ hours of labor without explanation. Also, beware of “diagnostic fees” that are not applied to the repair — a good shop will cred it. If the shop adds a “shop supplies” or “environmental disposal” fee that is a fixed percentage rather than itemized, question it.
- Additional tactic: Some shops will claim the entire fuse box “must” be replaced because “Honda doesn’t sell the relay separately.” This is true for the part, but the re-solder technique is a known, legitimate alternative. A refusal to consider re-soldering, especially if they claim it’s “unsafe” or “not a permanent fix,” without evidence, may be a tactic to inflate the bill. Thousands of these relays have been re-soldered successfully for over a decade.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- What to approve immediately: Authorize only a diagnostic hour (typically $60–120) that includes the key-on fuel pump prime test, the dash tap test, and a scan-tool live data capture during a cranking attempt. If the shop can replicate the no-start and the tap test instantly fixes it, you can approve the re-solder repair on the spot, but only with a clear line-item price. If the no-start cannot be replicated, approve an extended monitoring period where they keep the car for a few days with a fuel pump and main relay monitor setup — but set a cap on diagnostic cost ($200 max).
- What to reject outright: Reject any quote for a new fuel pump assembly, alternator, crankshaft sensor, or ECM reprogram until the main relay circuit has been definitively ruled out by the tests above, with data shown to you. Also reject any “fuel injection service” or “carbon cleaning” as a cure for an intermittent no-start — it has zero impact on an engine that doesn’t fire at all.
- When to get a second opinion: If the shop refuses to perform the tap test or cannot explain why they believe the main relay is not the issue, take the car to a Honda specialist or independent shop familiar with 8th-gen Civic electronics. A mobile diagnostic service that can do on-site re-soldering may also be a cost-effective option. If the dealer quotes over $800 for a MICU replacement without offering the re-solder alternative, get a second opinion from a well-reviewed independent shop; many will do the re-solder for under $250.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- System operation: The PGM-FI main relay controls power to the fuel pump, the ECM, and several sensors. When you turn the key to ON, the ECM briefly grounds the main relay coil, closing the contacts, which sends battery voltage to the fuel pump for a 2-second prime. Once the engine starts, the relay remains energized as long as the ECM sees cranking RPM (from the CKP) and then a running signal. If the relay contacts are open due to a cracked solder joint, the pump never runs, fuel pressure never builds, and the injectors won’t fire — hence crank-no-start with no DTCs, because the ECM can’t even power up its OBD-II monitor.
- Failure mechanism details: The relay is a small cube soldered onto the printed circuit board inside the under-dash fuse box. Over years of heat/cool cycles from the cabin heater and sunlight, plus mild vibration, the solder where the relay pins meet the PCB develops hairline cracks. In dry conditions, the cracks may still make contact. High humidity or a rainy day causes slight oxidation and expansion, opening the circuit. A physical jolt (cranking, driving, tapping) can reseat the connection momentarily, which explains why the car then runs perfectly. This is a pure electrical intermittent — not a fuel or spark problem.
- Prevention tips for the future: Once the relay is re-soldered with high-quality rosin-core solder (or the MICU is replaced), the fix is typically permanent. To prevent other age-related electrical gremlins, keep the cabin air filter fresh to avoid moisture buildup, and periodically check the cowl drain to ensure no water is entering the blower motor area. Additionally, applying dielectric grease to the under-dash fuse box connectors during reassembly will guard against future oxidation. Finally, if the car is parked outside, consider a cabin moisture absorber in humid climates to reduce dampness.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Specific part numbers: The under-dash fuse/relay box assembly (MICU) for a 2009 Honda Civic 1.8L is OEM part number 38200-SNA-A11 (verify by VIN; some LX/EX trims may vary). The main relay is not sold separately by Honda; it is internal to this box. However, the re-solder repair requires no new part — only skilled labor. If you must purchase the assembly, it is available at Honda dealers and reputable online OEM parts retailers. Aftermarket fuse boxes (Dorman or unbranded) are not recommended due to calibration and connector pinout differences that can cause parasitic draws or B-CAN communication errors.
- Why OEM is critical: The MICU contains not just the main relay but also the multiplex circuitry that talks to the gauge cluster, door locks, and immobilizer. Aftermarket units have a high failure rate. If re-soldering is performed on the OEM unit, the original Honda-specific firmware and calibration remain intact. This approach preserves the vehicle’s integrity and is far cheaper.
- Pricing sources and alternatives: New OEM MICU: check hondapartsnow.com, hondapartsconnection.com, or your local dealer’s online store; prices as of this writing are $285–$350. Used MICU from a salvage yard: $50–$100, but must be the exact same part number and require immobilizer reprogramming at the dealer, often costing as much as a new part after reprogramming. Therefore, the re-solder path is the most economical and direct.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Price comparison strategies: Before authorizing a MICU replacement, call three independent Honda shops and ask for a quote on “re-soldering the PGM-FI main relay in a 2009 Civic under-dash fuse box.” Most will quote a flat fee of $120–$200. Use these quotes to negotiate with your current shop: “I’ve received estimates from other Honda specialists to fix this exact problem for under $200 by re-soldering. Can you match that or explain why a full fuse box replacement is necessary today?”
- Labor justification questions: If the shop insists on replacing the MICU, ask them to show you the labor guide time for R&R of the fuse box. It’s usually 1.0–1.2 hours. Then ask, “Since the part is plug-and-play, why is there a diagnostic charge on top if we already know the main relay is at fault?” Push them to consolidate charges. Also, inquire about the cost difference between new and used, and ask if they’ll provide a warranty on a re-solder job (many offer a year).
- Walk-away points and leverage: Walk away immediately if they refuse to test the main relay with a tap test, or if they dismiss the re-solder as “not a real fix.” Your leverage is that you can easily have the car towed to another shop that will. Also, if the dealer quotes you a new MICU at full list price + maximum book time, negotiate by showing them the online OEM part price and ask for a price match; many will discount the part to keep the labor. If not, take the diagnosis data to an independent and buy the part online to have them install it.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: Cracked solder joints on the PGM-FI main relay inside the under-dash fuse box — 65% confidence. Symptoms match the textbook presentation of a moisture-sensitive intermittent no-start, no codes, and a known Honda pattern. The tap test will almost certainly confirm or deny this; thus the confidence is moderate until that data is obtained.
- Secondary cause: Intermittent open in the CKP sensor connector or sensor itself due to moisture — 15% confidence. While plausible, it would likely cause stalling when wet while driving, and often sets a pending code. The customer’s description of “runs fine once started” makes it less likely. A scan tool reading RPM during the failed crank will immediately rule this in or out.
- Tertiary cause: ECM ground corrosion or internal failure — 10% confidence. Much rarer, and usually presents with multiple symptoms (gauges flickering, no communication). If the main relay circuit tests fine and the fuel pump commands are present but no pump action, this becomes more probable. A thorough ground point inspection (G101, G102) at the left kick panel would be required.
- Quaternary cause: Ignition switch intermittent contact — 8% confidence. Would show up as a loss of all accessory power or starter operation, which is not reported. Still, a quick voltage drop test on the IGP circuit during cranking can eliminate it.
- All other causes: Fuel pump, immobilizer, aftermarket alarm, etc. — combined 2% confidence.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate actions required: As soon as practical, conduct the fuel pump prime and dash tap test yourself or have a shop do it. If the pump is silent during a no-start and tapping the dash panel restores it, you have your diagnosis without any further expense. Schedule the re-solder repair with a specialist. Do not drive the car if it fails to start repeatedly and leaves you stranded; have it towed if necessary to avoid multiple failed start attempts that could drain the new battery.
- Future maintenance schedule: After the relay is fixed, this system should be trouble-free for years. At the vehicle’s age, also inspect and clean the engine grounds (battery negative to chassis, engine to chassis strap) to prevent other electrical gremlins. Plan for a timing chain service if mileage is over 120k (though not related). Keep an eye on the under-dash area for any signs of moisture; fix any windshield or sunroof leaks promptly.
- Warning signs to monitor: Any future instance of the engine cranking but not firing — even once — should be investigated immediately with the tap test. A lingering fuel smell inside the car could indicate a developing fuel pump top-hat crack (another known Civic issue), but that is separate. If the engine ever stalls while driving, especially in wet conditions, that points more toward a CKP or ignition coil fault and requires a new diagnostic path.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Honda Technical Service Bulletin (TSB) 09-001 or 06-002: Although specific TSB numbers for the main relay re-solder are not publicly searchable, Honda has acknowledged intermittent no-start conditions on 2006–2011 Civics related to the PGM-FI main relay. Many dealer technicians are aware of this. You can ask any Honda service department to check for open bulletins on your VIN regarding “PGM-FI main relay intermittent operation.” Refusal to do so is unusual.
- NHTSA.gov complaint database: A search for “2009 Honda Civic crank no start rain” will reveal dozens of owner complaints describing exactly this scenario. While not a recall, the volume of reports supports the diagnosis and can be presented to a shop as evidence of a widespread issue.
- Honda-Tech forum and 8thCivic.com: These owner communities have thousands of posts documenting the re-solder fix with step-by-step photos. A thread titled “DIY: 8th gen Civic PGM-FI Main Relay Repair” is a canonical guide. The consistency of the symptoms and the repair outcome across over a decade of owner experiences provides robust independent verification. This is not sponsored content; it is crowd-sourced data from verified owners.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Immediately perform the key-on fuel pump prime listening test and the dash tap test at home to confirm the main relay failure, capturing video if possible. Use this evidence to direct any shop to the correct fix.
- If the tap test confirms the relay, authorize a re-solder repair only (budget $160–250) and explicitly decline any fuel pump, alternator, or full MICU replacement at this stage.
- If the no-start cannot be reproduced, have a shop install a fuel pump current monitor or a “no-start” data recorder that logs voltage at the pump connector over several days, targeting rainy conditions, to catch the failure in the act and isolate the open circuit definitively.
